docs.text: Takeaway: On the 1990 USGS map, Cuba sits at the southeastern end of the Ojo Alamo outcrop, where the sandstone is shallow; its top deepens northward past 1,000 and 3,000 ft. Research questions 4, 2, 3 What is plotted Crop of USGS Hydrologic Atlas HA-720-B, Figure 5 (approximate depth to the top of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone), with labels added Scope Cuba area and the eastern San Juan Basin (regional map, 1990) Data USGS Hydrologic Investigations Atlas HA-720-B (Thorn et al. 1990), Figure 5 (data/data5_ojo_alamo_sandstone_pub.pdf); public domain App page Cuba case study Code charts.ojo_alamo_depth_map() in analysis/charts.py How to read it and method: The map itself is unchanged; only the white labels and arrows are added. Brown is where the Ojo Alamo Sandstone crops out at the surface; each red line joins points where its top is the same depth below land surface, every 500 ft. 'Cuba' is the map's own town label. Dataset 5 is a scanned plate, so values are read by eye and nothing here is digitized. Findings: Measured: On the USGS map, Cuba sits at the southeastern end of the Ojo Alamo outcrop band, where the top of the sandstone is shallow; it deepens northward along the basin's eastern edge, past the 1,000-ft and 3,000-ft lines (read from the published map). Hypothesis: Because the Ojo Alamo is shallow at Cuba, shallow wells there can reach it, as the 148-ft Cuba school well did in 1957; whether Cuba's municipal wells use it today isn't established. Insufficient data: This is a 1990 regional interpretation at 1:1,000,000 scale, read by eye; it doesn't show current water levels, how much water the formation holds, or which formation Cuba's wells use.
docs.title: 10. ojo_alamo_depth_map

docs.text: Takeaway: Only 8 test events at 7-8 wells name these formations (7 Ojo Alamo, 1 San Jose; 1953-1977): too few to describe either formation, let alone compare them. Research questions 4, 2 What is plotted Every aquifer test recorded in the Ojo Alamo Sandstone or San Jose Formation (one dot per reported value), with published San Jose transmissivity for comparison Scope Sandoval County, including the Cuba area: tests 1-45 km from Cuba; published values from the San Juan Basin Data NM OSE aquifer tests (data/clean/aquifer_tests.csv); published values: Blandford et al. (2025), NMGS Guidebook 75, Table 1 (data/data6_cuba_mesa_member_of_san_jose_formation.pdf) App page Cuba case study Code charts.ojo_alamo_vs_san_jose() in analysis/charts.py How to read it and method: A test event is one well on one date; some events are reported on two rows (e.g. separate drawdown results), so n counts values. Two Ojo Alamo well names, 'Cuba Independent Rural School Well No 1' and '21.1W.28.143', share a location and depth and may be the same well. Open violet diamonds are published San Jose Formation transmissivity compiled in Blandford et al. (2025, Table 1): well SJ-2259, screened in the Cuba Mesa Member near Lindrith (estimated from specific capacity, assuming 70% well efficiency), and a range from two tests in Stone et al. (1983), location not given; both converted from m²/day. A value entered twice for the same test is drawn once. Depth to water and the two right panels use log scales. Blank panels mean the value wasn't recorded. The tests date from 1953-1977 and don't show which formation Cuba's municipal wells use today. Findings: Measured: Ojo Alamo depth to water: 18-24 ft at the well(s) within 5 km of Cuba, and 10-604 ft at wells 19-45 km away. Measured: San Jose: one test at one well (BIA-(RF)-033-2(10) Smelser Well, 9 km from Cuba, 1977): 51 ft to water, 206 ft deep, 100 ft²/day. That is close to the one published Cuba Mesa Member value near Lindrith (101 ft²/day at well SJ-2259, estimated from specific capacity) and inside the San Jose range from Stone et al. (1983), 43-118 ft²/day. Insufficient data: Comparing the formations needs more (and recent) tests, plus the Ojo Alamo thickness and extent maps in USGS HA-720-B (dataset 5), which is a scanned map plate not yet digitized.
docs.title: 11. ojo_alamo_vs_san_jose

docs.text: Takeaway: Rio Puerco at Cuba had measurable flow on all 4 visits in Apr-May and on none of the 6 visits from Aug to Mar. Research questions 3, 5, 6 What is plotted Each drop is one USGS field visit to station 08332525 (2019-2026); left by date (labeled with the month), right by month of year; not a continuous record Scope Cuba (measured at Cuba), surface water only (gage 2.3 km from the village center) Data USGS station 08332525, Rio Puerco at Cuba, NM (data/data4_channel-measurements.csv and data4_field-measurements.csv) App page Cuba case study Code charts.rio_puerco_visits() in analysis/charts.py How to read it and method: No line is drawn between visits because the river was not measured in between. 'No measurable flow' is what the visit recorded at that moment (the channel may still hold pools), not that the river was dry all season. docs.text: Almost nothing measures Cuba's groundwater. The nearest well measured more than once is about 38 km away. The answer to research question 3 is "insufficient data" until Cuba's municipal well records are collected. Four monitoring sites carry the county's trend story, all between Rio Rancho and Cochiti. They are indicators at those points, not a county average or a measure of how much water is left. Old, one-time records. Most aquifer tests date from 1930 to 2008 and record conditions on test day. Three proposal questions were dropped for lack of data: groundwater quality, acequias, and links between groundwater and surface water (see Not collected ). No geologic-region layer was collected either, so wells are grouped by nearest town and by the formation named in their aquifer tests. Simple statistics. Trends and correlations assume independent years; with serial correlation they look more certain than they are. Results are screening-level, not a groundwater model.

docs.text: 1. Data collection Lead: Dylan Gonzales This stage covers finding public datasets that can answer the research questions , downloading them, and recording where each one comes from. For each dataset, Dylan wrote a one-page brief. It covers what the dataset contains, which research questions it can help answer, which plots to make, and what the data can't show. A one-page guide compares all seven: Data plotting guide for datasets 1–7 (PDF) The briefs and the guide use the proposal's original nine research questions. Three of those were later dropped (see Not collected ) and the rest were renumbered: Q1 to Q4 are unchanged, the proposal's Q8 is now Q5, and its Q9 is now Q6. This page uses the new numbers. What the data can and can't show Together, the datasets are strongest for groundwater trends at monitored wells (Q1), well characteristics (Q2), comparing the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation (Q4), monitoring coverage and gaps (Q5), and dashboard indicators (Q6). The Rio Puerco measurements are the only data from Cuba itself, and they describe the river, not groundwater. None of them shows on its own whether Cuba's municipal aquifer is being depleted, or which formation Cuba's wells draw from. Every chart and caption should say whether it describes Cuba itself, Sandoval County, or the wider San Juan Basin. Datasets # Dataset From Relevance to Cuba Best for Brief 1 Groundwater-level statistics USGS Countywide; no Cuba wells Q1, Q5, Q6 PDF 2 Groundwater levels NM Bureau of Geology Countywide; nearest well about 24 miles from Cuba Q2, Q5, Q1 PDF 3 Aquifer sensitivity NM Environment Department Not established; the file has no locations Q6, once checked PDF 4 Rio Puerco at Cuba USGS At Cuba (river, not groundwater) Q3 (context), Q5, Q6 PDF 5 Ojo Alamo Sandstone USGS map plate Regional geology Q4, Q2 PDF 6 San Jose Formation near Lindrith NM Geological Society Regional geology Q4, Q2 PDF 7 Wells with well logs NM Office of the State Engineer 6 Sandoval well logs; Cuba link not verified Q2, Q5 PDF The raw files are in the repository's data/ folder , whose README lists each file, and Word versions of the briefs are in docs/files/ . 1. USGS groundwater-level statistics File: water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv Source: USGS Water Data statistics download USGS monthly and yearly statistics for 30 monitoring sites in Sandoval County (9 wells, 17 stream gages, 2 canals, and 2 reservoirs), with records from 1926 to 2026. Besides depth to groundwater, it covers streamflow, reservoir storage, suspended sediment, water temperature, and water quality (specific conductance, dissolved oxygen, pH, and turbidity). Dylan's brief covers the groundwater part: 9,462 records from 9 wells at four sites (Sandia, Lincoln Middle School, Bernalillo, and Dome Road), from about 1998 to 2026. Use for: depth-to-water trends at each well, a map of the wells, and a timeline of monitoring coverage. Cautions: none of the wells are in Cuba. Monthly, calendar-year, and water-year rows summarize the same measurements, so use one type at a time. A larger depth to water means a lower water table. 2. NM Bureau of Geology groundwater levels File: data2_groundwater_sandoval_county.csv Source: New Mexico Water Data: groundwater levels 456 depth-to-water measurements from 87 wells in Sandoval County, 1997 to 2019, from the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources. Each record has the well's location (UTM easting and northing), well depth, hole depth, measurement date, and depth to water below ground. Use for: a map of the wells, well depth compared with depth to water, time series for wells measured more than once, and measurement counts per well. Cautions: the nearest well is about 24 miles from Cuba. Many wells were measured only once, which can't show a trend. Check the UTM zone and datum before mapping. 3. Aquifer sensitivity File: data3_Aquifer_Sensitivity.csv Source: New Mexico Water Data: aquifer sensitivity ( map layer ) 613 mapped areas from the New Mexico Environment Department, each with a sensitivity class (339 Moderate, 152 High, and 122 Less) and the area's size and perimeter. The CSV has no coordinates or shapes, so it can't be mapped or matched to Cuba on its own. Use for: a sensitivity indicator on the dashboard (Q6), once the map layer is downloaded and it's clear what "sensitivity" measures. Cautions: the class counts are numbers of mapped areas, not shares of land. The file doesn't state the units for area and perimeter. 4. Rio Puerco at Cuba Files: data4_monitoring-location-metadata.csv , data4_field-measurements.csv , data4_channel-measurements.csv Source: USGS Water Data for the Nation: Rio Puerco at Cuba, NM (USGS-08332525) ( station map on the Water Quality Portal ) The only dataset measured at Cuba itself: USGS station 08332525 on the Rio Puerco. The three files hold the station's details and coordinates, 4 gage-height readings (2019 to 2024), and 10 streamflow measurements (2019 to 2026). Six of the streamflow visits found no flow, and the other four measured 6.89 to 20.40 cubic feet per second. Use for: surface-water context in the Cuba case study (Q3): a scatter plot of flow by date, a count of zero-flow and flowing visits, and a map of the station relative to Cuba. Cautions: these are occasional visits, not a continuous record, so zero-flow readings don't mean the river is dry all year. The station measures the river, not Cuba's groundwater or water supply. 5. Ojo Alamo Sandstone File: data5_ojo_alamo_sandstone_pub.pdf Source: USGS, Hydrogeology of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone in the San Juan Structural Basin (Hydrologic Atlas 720-B) A USGS map plate (1990) of the Ojo Alamo Sandstone across the San Juan Basin, showing depth to the top of the sandstone, its thickness, and wells completed in it. Use for: an annotated map, or a side-by-side comparison with the San Jose Formation (Q4). Cautions: this is a historical regional map, not current conditions, and it isn't a table to plot. It doesn't show that Cuba's wells draw from this formation. 6. San Jose Formation near Lindrith File: data6_cuba_mesa_member_of_san_jose_formation.pdf Source: Blandford et al. (2025), " San Jose Formation Hydrostratigraphy and Groundwater Conditions in the Vicinity of Lindrith, New Mexico ," New Mexico Geological Society Guidebook 75, pp. 235–246, doi:10.56577/FFC-75.235 A study of about 840 km² near Lindrith that uses more than 350 geophysical logs and 85 well-drilling logs. It identifies four water-bearing units in the San Jose Formation, maps the thickness of the Cuba Mesa Member, and maps groundwater levels. Use for: comparing with the Ojo Alamo Sandstone (Q4), and explaining which units wells reach (Q2). Cautions: the study is centered near Lindrith, not on Cuba's wells. The Cuba Mesa Member is a candidate water-bearing unit around Cuba, but the paper doesn't show that Cuba pumps from it. 7. Wells with well logs File: data7_Wells With Well Log Information.csv Source: NM Office of the State Engineer, New Mexico Water Rights Reporting System , "Wells With Well Log Information" report for the San Juan basin Drilling records for 6 wells in Sandoval County, drilled between 1978 and 2022, with location, borehole depth, depth where water was first found, and driller. They come from a San Juan basin download of 1,379 well logs across four counties, which Dylan's brief describes. Use for: comparing borehole depth with first-water depth (Q2), and mapping where well logs exist (Q5). Cautions: first-water depth was recorded on drilling day, not as a current water level. The file doesn't identify Cuba's municipal wells or the formation each well draws from. Other raw data in the repository ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv : New Mexico Office of the State Engineer aquifer-test records, 3,455 statewide and 179 in Sandoval County, including well depth, screened interval, geologic formation, and hydraulic properties such as transmissivity and storativity. It's cleaned into data/clean/aquifer_tests.csv (see Data cleaning ). Source: NM Office of the State Engineer, Hydrology Bureau: Aquifer Test Index (CSV export; added by Meckrem) sandoval_county_boundary.geojson : a simplified Sandoval County outline used as map context in the app and figures. Source: US Census Bureau 2010 cartographic boundary file, as redistributed in plotly/datasets geojson-counties-fips.json (FIPS 35043). A more detailed boundary wasn't collected (see below). Not collected These sources were identified in the proposal but weren't collected during the project. The report's Limitations section explains what their absence means for the findings. Cuba's municipal well records: well IDs, the formation each well draws from, pumping volumes, and water-level history, from the Village of Cuba or the NM Office of the State Engineer. Six of the seven briefs point to these records as the missing piece for answering whether Cuba's aquifer is being depleted (Q3). Aquifer sensitivity map layer: the map layer for dataset 3 and documentation of what its classes mean, to check whether it covers Cuba. Digital aquifer data near Cuba: USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data for the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation, to go beyond the maps in datasets 5 and 6. Water quality and salinity: the NM Bureau of Geology San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment and New Mexico Water Data records. Without them, the proposal's question on groundwater quality was dropped. Acequias: locations and service areas of acequias and community ditches from the NM Interstate Stream Commission. Without them, the proposal's questions on acequias and on links between groundwater and surface water were dropped. More water-level records: National Ground-Water Monitoring Network and Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network data. Shallow groundwater depth: the mean annual depth to groundwater for the shallow riparian aquifer dataset. County boundary: a detailed Sandoval County boundary layer. The maps use the simplified US Census outline above instead. docs.text: These sources were identified in the proposal but weren't collected during the project. The report's Limitations section explains what their absence means for the findings. Cuba's municipal well records: well IDs, the formation each well draws from, pumping volumes, and water-level history, from the Village of Cuba or the NM Office of the State Engineer. Six of the seven briefs point to these records as the missing piece for answering whether Cuba's aquifer is being depleted (Q3). Aquifer sensitivity map layer: the map layer for dataset 3 and documentation of what its classes mean, to check whether it covers Cuba. Digital aquifer data near Cuba: USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data for the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation, to go beyond the maps in datasets 5 and 6. Water quality and salinity: the NM Bureau of Geology San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment and New Mexico Water Data records. Without them, the proposal's question on groundwater quality was dropped. Acequias: locations and service areas of acequias and community ditches from the NM Interstate Stream Commission. Without them, the proposal's questions on acequias and on links between groundwater and surface water were dropped. More water-level records: National Ground-Water Monitoring Network and Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network data. Shallow groundwater depth: the mean annual depth to groundwater for the shallow riparian aquifer dataset. County boundary: a detailed Sandoval County boundary layer. The maps use the simplified US Census outline above instead.

Bottom line Are the available records enough to evaluate the concern that Cuba's main aquifer is approaching severe depletion? No: they can't confirm it or rule it out (Insufficient data). docs.text: 4. Streamlit app Lead: Meckrem Yousef Open the live app The interactive dashboard presents the project's results. It's built with Streamlit, pandas, and Plotly, and runs from ProjectApp.py in the repository. What the app shows Each page shows its charts with a one-line takeaway, what is plotted, the chart's scope (Cuba, the Cuba area, or Sandoval County), a caption, the findings labeled Measured , Hypothesis , or Insufficient data , and a "Data behind this chart" table with a CSV download. Charts are interactive: hover for exact values, drag to zoom, double-click to reset. They follow the app's light or dark theme. Six charts show small pictograms (wells, stream gages, river visits, rating balls); the Pictograph charts switch in the sidebar turns them off to show the plain versions used in the report (see Pictograph versions ). Page What it shows Research questions Home Project summary, links, and the research questions All County map Every site in the project's datasets on a map, colored by what it measures 1, 5 Groundwater levels Monthly water levels at the 9 USGS monitoring wells, their trends, and Placitas wells re-measured after 20 years 1 Wells and aquifers Well depth vs depth to water, depth to water by area, and aquifer-test properties by formation (choose the measurement from a menu) 2, 4 Cuba case study Key numbers, a short answer to research question 3, a map of sites near Cuba, the nearest record in each dataset, the USGS Ojo Alamo depth map around Cuba, Ojo Alamo vs San Jose tests, and Rio Puerco visits 3, 4 Data sources Dataset list and links, a timeline of monitoring coverage, a dataset-by-question evidence matrix, aquifer-sensitivity classes, and a table of groundwater-stress indicators 5, 6 Sandbox A test page with random data (not project results) - The chart code lives in analysis/ (see Analysis and visualizations ); each page file in app_pages/ calls show_chart(...) for its charts. The maps use the free CARTO basemap, which needs an internet connection. Running it yourself In GitHub Codespaces, open a codespace from the repository's Code button and the app starts automatically. On your own computer: pip install -r requirements.txt streamlit run ProjectApp.py How the live app updates The live app runs whatever is on the repository's main branch and redeploys within about a minute of each push.

Dylan Gonzales To be written. James Wauneka To be written. Micah Watkins I wrote the analysis code and made the project's charts. All of it lives in the analysis/ folder: loaders that bring every dataset into the team's shared column format (including the minimum preparation needed for the datasets that aren't cleaned yet), trend statistics (Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test), and one function per chart that returns the figure together with its takeaway, caption, scope, and labeled findings. The same functions feed the Streamlit pages, the report figures, and the documentation, so every number matches. I made 15 charts and figures covering all six research questions, wired them into the app's pages, and wrote a grading rubric from our proposal and Dylan's plotting guide to review and improve the charts. For six of them I also made pictograph versions (well cross-sections, a map of well pictograms sized by transmissivity, river-visit drops, rating balls, and unit charts), following Petar's suggestion, while keeping the plain versions for the report. Details are on the Analysis and visualizations page. Meckrem Yousef To be written. I built and maintain this documentation site and the repository's README files, and I narrowed the proposal's nine research questions to the six that the collected data can answer.
